title: Related Rates: the Chain Rule With Time Hidden

steps.body:
If two quantities are linked by an equation, then their **rates of change are linked too** — and the link is the chain rule, with **time as the hidden variable**.

Differentiate the equation with respect to **t**. Every variable is secretly a function of time, so every one of them picks up a dx/dt, exactly as implicit differentiation picked up a dy/dx.

It is the same move you already know, wearing a clock.

explanationVariants: A = πr² gives dA/dt = 2πr · (dr/dt). The chain rule charges you dr/dt because r is a function of t.
Without the dr/dt you have differentiated with respect to r, which answers a different question entirely.

widget.prompt: A circle's area is A = πr². Differentiate with respect to TIME.

options.label: dA/dt = 2πr · (dr/dt)
options.feedback: Right — r depends on t, so the chain rule attaches dr/dt. That factor is the whole subject.

options.label: dA/dt = 2πr
options.feedback: That is dA/dr — the derivative with respect to the RADIUS. Differentiating with respect to time adds a factor of dr/dt.

options.label: dA/dt = πr²
options.feedback: That is the area itself, undifferentiated.

options.label: dA/dt = 2π
options.feedback: The r has vanished. d/dr[πr²] = 2πr, and then the chain rule multiplies by dr/dt.

widget.prompt: Why related rates is not a new technique.

panels.title: You already did this
panels.body: In implicit differentiation, every y picked up a dy/dx because y was secretly a function of x. Here every variable picks up a d/dt because it is secretly a function of time. Same move, different hidden variable.

panels.title: The equation is the relation
panels.body: Geometry gives you the equation — the area of a circle, Pythagoras for a ladder, the volume of a sphere. Calculus never invents it. Your job is to FIND the right relation, and then differentiate it.

panels.title: Then substitute — but only at the END
panels.body: Differentiate first, with the variables still general. Only afterwards substitute the instant's numbers. Substituting first turns a variable into a constant, and its rate silently becomes zero.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep going — the third panel is the error that ruins these problems.
widget.successFeedback: Same chain rule, hidden variable is time. Differentiate FIRST, substitute LAST.

explanationVariants: If you substitute r = 3 before differentiating, A = 9π becomes a CONSTANT, and its derivative is 0 — which says the area never changes, which is absurd.
The radius is 3 only at one instant. It is not a constant, and treating it as one destroys the problem.

widget.prompt: To find dA/dt when r = 3, a student writes A = π(3²) = 9π and then differentiates. What goes wrong?

options.label: 9π is a constant, so its derivative is 0 — the substitution destroyed the very change being measured.
options.feedback: Right. r = 3 is true at ONE INSTANT, not always. Differentiate with r general, and substitute only at the end.

options.label: Nothing — it is a valid shortcut.
options.feedback: It gives dA/dt = 0, which claims the circle is not growing at all. The substitution froze the radius.

options.label: The 9π should be 6π.
options.feedback: The arithmetic is fine: π(3)² = 9π. The error is doing it too EARLY.

options.label: π should be differentiated too.
options.feedback: π really is a constant, and its derivative really is zero. The problem is that r was treated like one.

steps.body:
So the procedure is four lines, always:

1. **Draw it.** Label what varies; do not put numbers on the picture.
2. **Find the relation** between the quantities (geometry, not calculus).
3. **Differentiate with respect to t** — every variable pays a d/dt.
4. **Substitute the instant's values** and solve for the rate you want.

Substituting at step 2 instead of step 4 is the mistake that ruins the problem.

explanationVariants: dA/dt = 2πr · dr/dt. At the instant r = 3 with dr/dt = 2, that is 2π(3)(2) = 12π.
Differentiate in general; substitute the instant last. The radius was allowed to vary right up until the final line.

widget.prompt: A circle's radius grows at dr/dt = 2 cm/s. Find dA/dt when r = 3, as a multiple of π (give just the number).

commonErrors.feedback: That is 2πr at r = 3 without the dr/dt = 2. The chain rule multiplies by the rate: 2π(3)(2) = 12π.
That is the AREA (9π), not its rate of change.

hints: The relation is the volume of a sphere: V = (4/3)πr³.
Differentiate with respect to t: dV/dt = 4πr² · (dr/dt).
explanationVariants: Note that r² appears: the bigger the balloon, the faster the volume grows for the same growth in radius. That is the whole reason inflating a big balloon takes so much more air per centimetre.

widget.prompt: A spherical balloon's radius grows at 2 cm/s. Find dV/dt when r = 3, as a multiple of π (give just the number).

commonErrors.feedback: That is 4πr² at r = 3 without the dr/dt = 2. Multiply by the rate: 4π(9)(2) = 72π.
That is the volume-ish, not the rate. dV/dt = 4πr²·(dr/dt) = 72π.
Check the derivative: d/dr[(4/3)πr³] = 4πr², which is 36π at r = 3, and then × 2 = 72π.

steps.body: The chain rule, with a clock.
takeaways: Differentiate the RELATION with respect to t; every variable picks up a d/dt, exactly as in implicit differentiation.
Geometry supplies the equation. Calculus only differentiates it.
Substitute the instant's numbers LAST. Doing it first freezes a variable and sends its rate to zero.
steps.teaser: Next: the ladder that keeps sliding down the wall.

concept.body: Every letter in the equation is secretly a function of time. So when you differentiate with respect to t, every letter pays a d/dt — just as every y paid a dy/dx in implicit differentiation. And substitute the numbers only at the very END.

explanationVariants: The chain rule attaches ds/dt because s depends on t.

widget.prompt: A cube has volume V = s³. Differentiate with respect to time.

options.label: dV/dt = 3s²·(ds/dt)
options.feedback: Right — s depends on t, so the chain rule charges you ds/dt.

options.label: dV/dt = 3s²
options.feedback: That is dV/ds. With respect to TIME you must also multiply by ds/dt.
